extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in psychology and humor measurement (psychologists, psychometricians, positive psychology researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Information and criteria for using the State-Trait-Cheerfulness Inventory (STCI), a questionnaire measuring cheerfulness, seriousness, and bad mood as both trait dispositions and momentary states. Includes instrument format, scale lengths, psychometric notes, and administration time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerfulness (measured construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheerfulness is one of the three concepts assessed by the STCI as both a trait and a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered part of the temperamental basis of humor. Trait cheerfulness predicts easier induction into a cheerful mood (lower 'threshold in'), stronger experience of that state, and longer persistence in that state even under adverse circumstances (phenomena described as 'keeping' or 'losing one's humor').

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness (measured construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seriousness is one of the three concepts assessed by the STCI as both a trait and a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a temperamental dimension contrasting with cheerfulness; assessed in both the trait (STCI-T) and state (STCI-S) versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad mood (measured construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad mood is one of the three concepts assessed by the STCI as both a trait and a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessed alongside cheerfulness and seriousness to capture the affective/temperamental profile relevant to sense of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: State vs. Trait measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The STCI measures cheerfulness, seriousness, and bad mood as both states (STCI-S) and traits (STCI-T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits are conceptualized as dispositions that facilitate activation of the homologous states; the trait instrument captures stable disposition while the state instrument captures momentary mood and is sensitive to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale length / items per scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Item counts differ between trait and state versions: the STCI-T and STCI-S use 20 and 10 items per scale, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trait part has longer scales (20 items per scale) while the state part uses shorter scales (10 items per scale), reflecting the trait/state distinction in measurement granularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response format
rubrics_metrics.description: Both parts utilize a 4-point answer format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchors run from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' (4-point Likert-style response).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychometric characteristics: reliability and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The trait part is reported as reliable; the state part is reported as sensitive to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trait scales are suitable for measuring stable dispositions (reliability emphasized), whereas state scales are suitable for detecting experimental or situational changes (responsiveness/sensitivity emphasized). The scales have been validated in a variety of studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration time
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated completion times differ for the two versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trait (STCI-T) version takes approximately 10 minutes to complete and the state (STCI-S) version takes approximately 5 minutes.
